title: [codex] Improve chat reliability and keyboard autoscroll
body:
## Summary

This PR improves two rough edges that showed up during real device testing:

- Keeps the latest messages visible when the keyboard opens by scrolling to a stable bottom anchor after focus and keyboard frame changes.
- Makes private-message routing more robust when peers are represented by either their full Noise public key or their short mesh peer ID.
- Prevents BLE receive-side deduplication from dropping distinct packets that share the same sender, packet type, and millisecond timestamp.

## Root Cause

The BLE receive deduplication key only used sender, timestamp, and packet type. During quick message bursts, two distinct packets could share those fields and the later packet would be treated as a duplicate.

Private chat delivery also mixed full Noise public keys and short peer IDs across routing, handshakes, queued outbox messages, read receipts, delivery ACKs, and reachability checks. That made some paths fail to find the established session or reachable transport even though the peer was present.

## Details

- Uses payload-aware packet IDs for BLE deduplication and self-broadcast tracking.
- Normalizes Noise session operations and queued private payloads to the short peer ID.
- Preserves the original full destination ID when flushing queued messages, while using a canonical short-ID outbox key.
- Accepts inbound private packets addressed to either the local short peer ID or the local full Noise static public key.
- Extends Nostr reachability checks to match full and short peer IDs.
- Adds regression tests for burst packet deduplication, local recipient addressing, and full/short private-message routing.

title: Add double-ratchet encryption for Nostr relay DMs
body:
## Summary

This adds double-ratchet encryption for Nostr relay private messages, backed by a vendored local `NdrFfi` Swift package from [nostr-double-ratchet](https://github.com/mmalmi/nostr-double-ratchet) `v0.0.97-3-g5fa8dbb` (`5fa8dbb7d4a2ea21e448e5fa220f655030de12f2`).

## Why double ratchet

- Relay DMs are long-lived and asynchronous; double ratchet gives per-message key evolution instead of relying on one long-term NIP-17 key agreement for the whole conversation.
- If the receiver's long-term/main key is compromised, plain NIP-17 can expose received relay history and future received messages. Double ratchet limits that exposure and can recover future received messages once the active compromise is gone.
- It gives disappearing messages a cryptographic foundation: expiration policy can live inside the protected payload while old relay-stored ciphertext becomes less useful as message keys advance.

## What changed

- Adds the `NdrFfi` package and XCFramework slices for macOS, iOS device, and iOS simulator.
- Adds NDR session handling inside the existing Nostr relay DM path.
- Adds Nostr identity bridging, message/reaction/receipt routing support, and cross-device automation tests.
- Keeps automation-only hooks behind debug/macOS test wiring.

## Vendored FFI note

This PR vendors prebuilt `NdrFfi` artifacts from [nostr-double-ratchet](https://github.com/mmalmi/nostr-double-ratchet) so the app can use one shared Rust implementation across macOS/iOS/Android without requiring every app build to install Rust, UniFFI, Apple cross-compilation targets, and the Android NDK. The vendored artifacts are pinned to a source commit and include provenance metadata. Apple static archives are stripped with `xcrun strip -S` to remove DWARF debug info while preserving link symbols, and the mobile build keeps UniFFI bindgen CLI dependencies out of the app-facing FFI library.

If preferred before merge, this can be changed to build `ndr-ffi` from source during CI/app builds, or to reference the `nostr-double-ratchet` repo as a pinned submodule/dependency. A native Swift/Kotlin implementation is also possible, but I avoided that here because duplicating the double-ratchet protocol across app codebases would increase security and compatibility risk compared with using the same tested Rust implementation everywhere.

## Verification

- `./localPackages/NdrFfi/build-apple.sh /Users/sirius/src/nostr-double-ratchet`
- `swift test` in `localPackages/NdrFfi`
- `cargo test -p ndr-ffi` from the source [nostr-double-ratchet](https://github.com/mmalmi/nostr-double-ratchet) checkout
- `xcodebuild -project bitchat.xcodeproj -scheme 'bitchat (macOS)' -configuration Debug -derivedDataPath build/codex-macos-debug-ndr CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY= build`

title: RFC: Private Swap Meet Feature Proposal
body:
## Summary

In crisis scenarios, people need to trade resources — medicine, batteries, SIM cards — but finding a match today means announcing what you have and need to a group chat, exposing your full inventory to everyone and hoping the right person sees it.

Swap Meet flips this. Users configure their wants and haves once and activate swap mode. Their device silently checks every nearby peer in the background. You're only notified when there's a mutual match — no broadcasting, no scrolling, no negotiation until there's something to negotiate.

## Cryptographic approach

The protocol uses Diffie-Hellman PSI over Ristretto255. Each party blinds their items with a secret exponent, exchanges the blinded values over BLE, and both sides double-exponentiate to find matches. Non-matching items are computationally indistinguishable from random. The full exchange is ~4KB for 20 items each.

Full RFC: [`docs/rfc-dh-psi-swap-meet.md`](https://github.com/bigwill/bitchat/blob/dh-psi-swap-meet/docs/rfc-dh-psi-swap-meet.md)

title: fix: use country-level resolution for low-precision geohashes
body:
## Summary

Fixes #887 — When bookmarking a 2-character geohash channel (e.g., "gc" for United Kingdom), the resolved location name showed "England" instead of "United Kingdom".

**Root cause:** `resolveCompositeAdminName()` and `nameForGeohashLength()` in `LocationStateManager.swift` prioritized `administrativeArea` (province/state) over `country` for low-precision geohashes (≤2 characters). A 2-char geohash covers a region/country, so the country name should take precedence.

## Changes

- `resolveCompositeAdminName()` — swapped `if/else` priority: check `pm.country` first, fall back to `pm.administrativeArea`
- `nameForGeohashLength()` — changed `case 0...2` from `pm.administrativeArea ?? pm.country` to `pm.country ?? pm.administrativeArea`

## How it works now

| Geohash | Before | After |
|---------|--------|-------|
| `gc` (UK) | "England" or "England and Scotland" | "United Kingdom" |
| `u3` (France) | Administrative area name | "France" |

Higher-precision geohashes (3+ chars) are unaffected — they continue to resolve to province/city/neighborhood as appropriate.

## Test plan

- [ ] Bookmark a 2-char geohash channel → verify country name is displayed
- [ ] Bookmark a 3+ char geohash channel → verify province/city name still works
- [ ] Remove and re-bookmark to clear cached names

title: [codex] Refactor app runtime and ownership architecture
body:
## What changed

This PR completes the app-layer architecture pass on top of the `architecture-v2` branch.

It:
- moves peer identity, encryption, verification, and stable peer-ID mapping into `PeerIdentityStore`
- moves geohash presence, nicknames, and teleport state into `LocationPresenceStore`
- rewires `AppRuntime`, feature models, and command handling to read through those owners instead of relying on `ChatViewModel` state bags or global channel state
- further decomposes `ChatViewModel` into focused coordinators for public chat, private chat, Nostr, verification, media, delivery, composer, formatting, and peer identity responsibilities
- adds focused architecture coverage for the new ownership layer and keeps the smoke harness aligned with the extracted app shell

## Why

The app was still carrying too much duplicated ownership between `ChatViewModel`, feature models, and shared managers. That made state flow harder to reason about and made follow-on changes riskier than they needed to be.

This refactor makes the app-side architecture much more explicit:
- app/runtime state has clearer owners
- feature models consume app-layer state rather than peeking through large view-model bags
- `ChatViewModel` is much thinner and closer to an adapter than an everything-object

## Impact

User-facing behavior should stay the same, but the app layer is now:
- easier to maintain
- easier to test
- safer to evolve without accidental coupling

This PR intentionally does **not** rework the transport/BLE core yet.

[vuln] Fix announce trust anchoring
body:
## Summary
This PR fixes the BLE identity-spoofing path by removing unauthenticated signing-key trust, requiring a trusted signing key for public content, revoking that trust immediately when a user removes verification, clearing stale stored signing keys during manual fingerprint verification, clearing the active session's in-memory public signing-key trust during manual verification, and persisting cryptographic identities so returning peers can be authenticated consistently across app restarts.

## Why this was a security problem
The original flow had several related trust failures:
- announce packets could introduce an attacker-controlled signing key before any trusted binding existed
- manual fingerprint verification could persist or preserve a signing key even though the user had only verified the Noise fingerprint, not the public-message signing key
- once a peer was treated as trusted in memory, public messages and file transfers were accepted without enforcing a valid packet signature, and that in-memory trust could outlive later verification removal or manual re-verification
- the code also treated cryptographic identities as if they were durable trusted state even though they were not actually persisted, which made the returning-peer trust path inconsistent

That meant a nearby attacker could poison the public-identity trust anchor ahead of verification, inject unsigned public content under a trusted peer identity, survive manual re-verification inside the same live session, or rely on mismatched runtime-vs-persisted trust behavior after restart.

## Fix
- keep first-contact announces discoverable, but do not retain or trust the advertised signing key unless the announce authenticates against an already trusted signing key
- make manual `Mark Verified` persist only the verified Noise identity; it no longer anchors a public-message signing key
- explicitly clear any previously stored signing key when the user manually verifies a fingerprint, so older poisoned state does not survive re-verification
- explicitly clear the active session's in-memory trusted signing key when a user manually verifies or removes verification, so public identity trust is not silently retained across trust-state changes
- keep QR verification as the OOB path that can safely persist the signing key, since the QR payload carries that key through the verified challenge/response flow
- require a valid packet signature from a trusted signing key for public messages and file transfers, including already-known in-memory peers
- persist cryptographic identities in the encrypted identity cache so the returning-peer authentication path is actually durable and consistent with the runtime trust model
- re-check persisted verification state before trusting active-session signing keys, so removing verification revokes public trust immediately without requiring reconnect or restart
- clarify the fingerprint screen so it distinguishes fingerprint verification from trusted public signing-key verification

## User impact
- spoofed first-contact announces no longer seed a trusted signing key
- unsigned public messages and file transfers from trusted-looking peers are rejected
- removing verification now revokes public signed-content trust immediately for the active session
- manual fingerprint verification no longer preserves either stored or in-memory public signing-key trust
- returning peers can still be authenticated after restart because the trusted cryptographic identity is now actually persisted
- manual fingerprint verification still marks the Noise identity verified, but public-message authentication now depends on a signing key that was actually verified out of band
- QR-verified peers continue to work for authenticated public identity and content

## Validation
- `swift test --filter BLEServiceCoreTests`
- `swift test --filter ChatViewModelVerificationTests`
- `swift test --filter SecureIdentityStateManagerTests`
- `swift test --filter ProtocolContractTests`
- `swift test --filter VerificationServiceTests`

title: fix: Offline message queue for airplane-mode BLE chat
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1039 — Private messages fail immediately with "unreachable" in airplane mode (BLE-only) instead of being queued for delivery.

### Root cause

The message router rejected messages outright when `isPeerReachable` returned false (time-window heuristic expired), and even when messages were queued, the flush path had the same reachability gate — creating a deadlock where offline messages could never be sent.

### What changed

- **Always-queue-first architecture**: `sendPrivate` always appends to the outbox then flushes, instead of branching between send-or-queue. Messages are never rejected with "unreachable" — they get `.sending` status and wait for the peer to connect.
- **Delivery-ack-based removal**: Messages stay in the outbox until a delivery or read ack confirms receipt, instead of being removed the moment they're handed to a transport. This prevents silent message loss when a Noise session is stale on reconnect.
- **Transport return value**: `sendPrivateMessage` now returns `Bool` — `true` when encrypted and broadcast, `false` when internally queued (e.g., BLE waiting for Noise handshake). The outbox only applies the resend cooldown on `true`, so pending-handshake messages are retried on every flush.
- **Flush after Noise handshake**: New `didEstablishEncryptedSession` delegate callback triggers an outbox flush once the encrypted session is ready, covering the gap where `didConnectToPeer` fires before the handshake completes.
- **PeerID normalization**: All outbox keys go through `toShort()` to prevent mismatches between 16-hex and 64-hex peer ID formats.
- **Deduplication**: BLE's internal `pendingMessagesAfterHandshake` deduplicates by messageID to prevent repeated flush attempts from creating duplicates.

### Flush triggers (redundancy for reliability)

| Trigger | When it fires |
|---------|--------------|
| `sendPrivate()` | User sends a message — immediate flush attempt |
| `didConnectToPeer()` | BLE peer reconnects |
| `didEstablishEncryptedSession()` | Noise handshake completes (primary path) |
| `didUpdatePeerList()` | Every BLE announce — fallback when `didConnectToPeer` is suppressed |

## Test plan

- [x] Existing `MessageRouterTests` updated for new always-queue behavior
- [x] New tests: flush-on-reconnect, delivery confirmation, message ordering, cooldown reset, transport `false` return handling, post-handshake flush
- [x] `ChatViewModelExtensionsTests` updated: unreachable peer now gets `.sending` instead of `.failed`
- [x] Manual test: two iPhones in airplane mode with Bluetooth on — send PM, verify delivery after BLE connection establishes

body:
## AI Provider Architecture

Adds the foundation for AI-assisted messaging in bitchat, designed around the same principles as the existing mesh networking: prefer the most private option, fall back gracefully, and always tell the user what happened.

### Why AI in bitchat

Bitchat already solves a hard problem: communication when infrastructure fails. But there is a gap in the current design. A person who is offline, isolated, and unable to reach any peers on the mesh has a working radio with nobody on the other end. On-device AI fills that gap. Even with no connectivity at all, a local language model (e.g. something like Tiny Aya from Cohere Labs) gives the user something genuinely useful — a companion that can help them think through a situation, draft a message for when connectivity returns, translate between languages, or simply be present when no one else is. 

This matters most in disaster scenarios, but the value does not have to stop there. The same capability creates a reason to open bitchat every day, not just when things go wrong. Daily engagement is what keeps a mesh network alive —nodes that are powered on and in range are the mesh. And a live mesh makes the AI itself more resilient: when internet access is available, inference requests can route through Nostr to more powerful remote models; when it is not, the local model is already warm and ready. AI utility drives engagement, engagement sustains the mesh, and the mesh makes AI more private and more available. Each piece reinforces the others.

### Architecture

- **AIProvider protocol**: The abstraction every backend conforms to.
  ChatViewModel never knows which concrete provider is active.
- **AIProviderRouter**: Manages provider selection, fallback, and consent.
  Bridged providers require explicit user consent before any data leaves
  the device.
- **MLXAIProvider**: On-device inference using Apple's MLX framework.
  Selects the best model for the device's RAM. WiFi-only downloads.
  Actor-isolated inference. Auto-unloads after 5 minutes of inactivity.
- **NostrBridgeAIProvider**: Stub for a future NIP-90 DVM bridge. The
  design supports a DVM backed by a service like PPQ.ai, paid with
  Cashu ecash from the bitchat app, with requests and responses flowing
  through the same Nostr relays bitchat already uses for messaging.
  Currently unavailable; architecture is ready without changes.
- **AIModelConfig**: All product decisions (model URLs, sizes, RAM
  requirements) live in config structs, not code.

### Privacy

The consent gate is not optional. The router will never send data through a bridged provider without explicit user permission. Local inference requires no consent because nothing leaves the device.

### Integration

- `ChatViewModel+AI.swift` extends the existing ViewModel via extension
- AI config and router are static on the extension — zero changes to
  the existing initializer or any existing files
- AI responses use the existing BitchatMessage model
- No existing files modified

### What's not in this PR

- Actual MLX inference (placeholder returns test string; real MLXLLM
  calls shown in comments, ready to uncomment once SPM deps are added)
- Nostr bridge implementation (stub only, designed for NIP-90 DVMs)
- MLX Swift package dependencies (added separately to avoid bloating
  this PR)
- UI wiring into ContentView (next PR)
- Streaming responses
- Cashu wallet integration for paid bridge queries

### Testing

Router tests verify consent gating, fallback logic, and error cases using mock providers. All existing tests unaffected. Build passes (only pre-existing Localizable.xcstrings errors remain).

### Pre-existing build fixes (unrelated to AI feature)

This PR also fixes two bugs on main that prevent compilation:

1. Localizable.xcstrings: Removed orphaned %@ key that only contains special characters — Swift cannot derive a valid symbol name from it, causing "Unable to derive a symbol name from this key" errors that block the entire bitchat module from compiling.
2. Package.swift: Narrowed .process("Noise") to .process("Noise/NoiseTestVectors.json") — the broad path causes NoiseProtocolTests.swift (a source file) to be treated as a bundle resource, triggering a build warning.

Both are reproducible on main independent of this PR.

Note: There is also a separate pre-existing issue where the Arti xcframework only ships arm64 slices, so the project cannot link on Intel Macs. That is not addressed here.

title: feat: add Lightning and Cashu payment packets to the Noise protocol layer
body:
## What this does

bitchat already detects bolt11 invoices and Cashu tokens in plain text (via `MessageFormattingEngine`) and renders them as chips (`PaymentChipView`). This PR adds a **protocol-level payment layer** — structured TLV packets sent inside the existing Noise-encrypted channel, rather than embedded in chat text.

## Two new `NoisePayloadType` cases

```swift
case lightningPaymentRequest = 0x20  // BOLT11 invoice
case cashuToken              = 0x21  // Cashu eCash bearer token
```

Both are carried inside `MessageType.noiseEncrypted` — network observers cannot distinguish payment traffic from regular private messages.

## `LightningPaymentRequestPacket`

Structured BOLT11 request with:
- `requestID` — stable UUID for delivery receipts and UI deduplication  
- `invoice` — full BOLT11 string (UInt16 length field, supports up to 65 KB)  
- `memo` — optional human-readable description  
- `amountSat` — optional decoded amount so UI can display without decoding the invoice  
- `expiresAt` — optional Unix timestamp so the UI can mark expired invoices

## `CashuTokenPacket`

Cashu eCash bearer tokens — the token string **is** the money. Neither sender nor relay needs internet. The receiver redeems at the mint when they next have connectivity.

This enables **genuinely offline Bitcoin transfers over Bluetooth mesh** — valuable for remote areas, events without cell coverage, and humanitarian use cases where connectivity is unreliable.

## Why structured packets over raw text?

| | Raw text (current) | Structured packet (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| Amount visible before wallet opens | ❌ must decode invoice | ✅ `amountSat` field |
| Expiry-aware UI | ❌ | ✅ `expiresAt` field |
| Delivery receipts | ❌ can't correlate | ✅ stable `requestID` |
| Chat thread stays clean | ❌ invoice string in message | ✅ separate payload type |
| Deduplication on re-relay | ❌ | ✅ `requestID` / `transferID` |

## Wire compatibility

Unknown `NoisePayloadType` bytes are already skipped gracefully by the existing Noise dispatch — **older clients compile and run without changes**. The new `BitchatDelegate` methods have default empty implementations for the same reason.

## TLV encoding

Follows the established `BitchatFilePacket` pattern with UInt16 big-endian length fields (supports strings up to 65 KB — necessary since BOLT11 invoices regularly exceed 255 bytes, which rules out the 1-byte length used in `PrivateMessagePacket`).

title: Revert Noise nonce size to 4 bytes for backward compatibility
body:
## Summary
This pull request addresses a critical regression introduced in commit `f41a390` where the Noise protocol nonce size was increased from 4 bytes to 8 bytes to better comply with the Noise specification.

## The Issue
Changing the nonce size is a breaking change for the wire protocol. Old clients expect 4 bytes, while new clients were sending 8 bytes (and vice versa). This caused decryption failures for all encrypted Direct Messages between clients running different versions.

## The Fix
This PR reverts the nonce size to **4 bytes** to restore backward compatibility.
Specifically, it:
1.  Sets `NONCE_SIZE_BYTES` back to 4.
2.  Restores the logic to extract a 4-byte big-endian nonce from the payload.
3.  Restores the logic to serialize the nonce into 4 bytes.
4.  Re-enables the safety check to ensure the nonce does not exceed `UInt32.max`.

## Notes
Crucially, this PR **does not** revert the other security improvements made in `f41a390`, such as:
*   Constant-time key validation and comparisons.
*   Safe arithmetic in the replay window check.
*   Sensitive state clearing.

This ensures we keep the security hardening where possible without breaking the protocol.

title: fix BCH-01-004: rate-limit subscription-triggered announces
body:
## Summary
- Fixes Cure53 audit finding BCH-01-004 (Medium severity): Device fingerprinting via forced disclosure
- Adds rate-limiting to prevent rapid device enumeration attacks
- Without this fix, attackers could enumerate ~120 bitchat devices/minute by rapid subscribe/disconnect cycles

## Problem
When a BLE central connects and subscribes to the bitchat characteristic, the peripheral automatically responds with a full announce packet containing:
- User's Noise public key (stable identifier)
- Nickname
- List of connected peers (social graph)

This enables rapid enumeration where an attacker systematically scans, connects, subscribes, captures identity info, and moves to the next device.

## Solution
Implements per-central rate-limiting with exponential backoff:
- **Minimum 2-second interval** between subscription-triggered announces per central
- **Exponential backoff (2x)** up to 30 seconds for rapid reconnects from same central
- **Suppression after 5 rapid attempts** - likely an enumeration attack
- **60-second tracking window** with automatic cleanup of stale entries
- Rate-limit state cleared during panic mode

## Configuration (TransportConfig.swift)
```swift
bleSubscriptionRateLimitMinSeconds: 2.0
bleSubscriptionRateLimitBackoffFactor: 2.0
bleSubscriptionRateLimitMaxBackoffSeconds: 30.0
bleSubscriptionRateLimitWindowSeconds: 60.0
bleSubscriptionRateLimitMaxAttempts: 5
```

## Impact
- Without rate-limiting: ~120 devices/minute enumeration possible
- With rate-limiting: Max ~30 devices/minute, with backoff making repeated attempts even slower
- Legitimate mesh operation preserved (directed packet flush, announce rebroadcast still happen)

## Test plan
- [x] All 378 tests pass (374 existing + 4 new)
- [x] Added `SubscriptionRateLimitTests.swift` verifying:
  - Configuration values are sensible
  - Exponential backoff calculation works correctly  
  - Rate limiting significantly slows enumeration attacks

## Summary
- Fixes Cure53 audit finding BCH-01-002 (Medium severity): Files persisted on filesystem facilitate DoS
- Incoming files are now held in memory via `PendingFileManager` instead of being auto-saved to disk
- Users must explicitly accept files before they are written, preventing attackers from exhausting device storage

title: feat: Source routing v2
body:
implements same source routing feature as on android: https://github.com/permissionlesstech/bitchat-android/pull/445

- announce direct neighbors in `ANNOUNCE` packet for gossip
- source-route packets with a valid route to the recipient
- forward source-routed packets if we're an intermediate hop

changes:
- only v2 packets support source routing
- v2 packets have a `route` field in the header
- `route` includes only intermediate hops, first is `senderID`, last is `recipientID`
- clients use an edge for routing only if both edges have confirmed the edge: for `A <--> B` will only be used if both `A` and `B` have announced their edge
- this also guarantees backwards compat: only updated clients with support for source routing will have announced the edge, which means they will also be able to decode a v2 packet with a route
